title: Stigma among health professionals towards patients with substance use disorders and its consequences for healthcare delivery: Systematic review

claims.statement: In studies published from 2000 to 2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and eight other European countries, mostly surveys in which health professionals reported their own attitudes, many professionals described negative attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug problems, or regarded them less well than patients with other conditions, more often outside specialist drug and alcohol services, while several studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes; whether such attitudes make the care these patients receive worse was examined in only a few studies, whose results point different ways. A systematic review of 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples; 12 from Australia, 7 from the UK and 5 from the US; 20 quantitative, mostly questionnaires at one time point, five interview or focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two using observation) gave no count or pooled estimate of how common negative attitudes were. Among its examples: among 866 professionals in eight European countries, regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with patients with depression or diabetes, and lowest among doctors outside specialist drug and alcohol services; in a vignette study, professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness; and at least six study summaries in the review's table describe attitudes as moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive (editors' count). More contact, experience, training and support went with more positive attitudes, in data collected at one time. On consequences for care: clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney who perceived more discrimination by staff were less likely to complete treatment (a mixed-methods study of 92 clients, attributed in the review's text to the wrong paper by the same team); two qualitative studies suggested that clinicians may impose their beliefs on patients, and described district nurses making shorter, task-focused visits; among 2,864 patients with HIV, 17.1% of them currently injecting drugs, physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reports of problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or access; and the one included study that observed care, 683 visits to nine psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986, found better care for patients with substance use problems than for other patients on all four criteria, a result the review's text does not mention (van Boekel et al., 2013). The review searched three databases in English and Dutch, excluded studies from Asia, Africa and South America and studies of training, weighted all studies equally whatever their response rate (31% to 92% where given), and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 by the study card; its abstract's statements that negative attitudes reduced patients' empowerment and treatment outcomes rest on two qualitative studies. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimate and no count of studies by direction. As reported by van Boekel et al. (2013): 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples); regard lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems among 866 professionals in 8 European countries; at least 6 of the study summaries describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes (editors' count of Table 5); 5 papers link more experience or contact with more positive attitudes. Consequences: perceived staff discrimination predicted not completing treatment (92 clients, Sydney); physicians' attitudes not associated with patients' reports of care (2,864 patients with HIV, 373 physicians; 23.2% of the patients had physicians with negative attitudes towards people who inject drugs); better care for patients with substance use problems on all 4 criteria in 683 observed emergency visits (California, 1985–1986).
